procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Meghalaya at Shillong
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 29.09.2023 passed in Bail Application No. 38/2023
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Meghalaya at Shillong granted bail on 29.09.2023 in connection with FIR No.06(02)23. The bail application was moved by the son of the accused-Smt.X, on her behalf.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Meghalaya filed a Special Leave Petition challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court disposed of the Special Leave Petition because the High Court's grant of bail did not satisfactorily consider the twin conditions under Section 37(1)(b)(ii) of the NDPS Act.

directions: The impugned order is set aside.
The accused-Smt.X shall surrender before the trial Court within a week from today and in case of her failure to do so, she shall be taken into custody in accordance with law.
Upon such surrender/production of the accused before the trial Court, it shall cancel the bail bond of the accused and discharge the sureties.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in granting bail to the accused solely on the ground that she was suffering from HIV, without adverting to the mandate under Section 37(1)(b)(ii), NDPS Act, and without taking in view the quantity of the contraband substance.

facts: The accused, who is HIV positive, was arrested for possessing 1.040 kgs of heroin, a commercial quantity under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act.
The accused had been involved in offences under the NDPS Act on more than one occasion.
The High Court granted bail to the accused solely on the ground that she was suffering from HIV.
The High Court's order did not consider the strict bail conditions mandated by the NDPS Act.
law: Section 37 of the NDPS Act imposes strict limitations on granting bail for offences involving commercial quantities of contraband.
To grant bail under Section 37, a court must record its satisfaction on two mandatory conditions (the "twin conditions"):
1. There are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty of the offence.
2. The accused is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
Recording a finding on these twin conditions is a "sine qua non" (an essential prerequisite) for granting bail under the NDPS Act, and a liberal approach is impermissible.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed a "very serious lapse" by granting bail without considering or recording a finding on the mandatory twin conditions of Section 37.
The Court emphasized that the large commercial quantity of heroin and the accused's history of similar offences made the application of Section 37's rigors even more critical.
It held that being an HIV patient cannot be the sole reason to grant bail and bypass the strict statutory requirements of the NDPS Act.
The Court reasoned that allowing bail on such grounds would send a wrong message that having a disease is a "license to indulge in such serious offences with impunity."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in granting bail. Because the mandatory twin conditions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act were not considered or satisfied, the accused was not entitled to be released on bail, and the High Court's order was overturned.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in granting bail to the accused solely on the ground that she was suffering from HIV, without adverting to the mandate under Section 37(1)(b)(ii), NDPS Act, and without taking in view the quantity of the contraband substance.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (State of Meghalaya) argued that the High Court was incorrect in granting bail to the accused.
The High Court's decision was based solely on the ground that the accused was suffering from HIV.
The High Court failed to consider the mandatory conditions for bail under Section 37(1)(b)(ii) of the NDPS Act.
The High Court also did not take into account the quantity of the contraband substance involved.

cases.case_name: State of Kerala and Ors. v. Rajesh and Ors.
cases.principle: To reiterate that the court is bound to ensure the satisfaction of the twin conditions under Section 37(1)(b)(ii) of the NDPS Act before granting bail.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When considering bail under the NDPS Act, a court is bound to ensure the satisfaction of the twin conditions under Section 37(1)(b)(ii), which are cumulative and not alternative.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court committed a very serious lapse by granting bail without considering the mandatory provisions of Section 37 of the NDPS Act. When an accused is involved in an offence with a commercial quantity of a contraband substance, as in this case where the quantity of heroin was 1.040 Kgs, granting bail solely on the ground that the accused is an HIV patient is impermissible. This reason alone cannot be used to enlarge the accused on bail, especially when the twin conditions under Section 37—that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail—are not satisfied.
legal_tests_applied: For offences involving a commercial quantity of narcotic drugs, granting bail requires the mandatory satisfaction of the twin conditions under Section 37(1)(b)(ii) of the NDPS Act, which are cumulative and not alternative.
The court must find that there are 'reasonable grounds' to believe that the accused is not guilty of the alleged offence and that they are not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
The term 'reasonable grounds' means something more than prima facie grounds and contemplates substantial and probable causes for believing that the accused is not guilty of the alleged offence.
Recording a finding that satisfies the mandate under Section 37 of the NDPS Act is a sine qua non (an essential condition) for granting bail to an accused under the Act.
policy_considerations: Granting bail solely on the ground that the accused is an HIV patient would give a wrong message to society that being a patient of such a disease is a license to indulge in serious offences with impunity.

While considering bail applications under the NDPS Act, courts cannot be oblivious to the objects and reasons for the enactment, and a liberal approach that ignores the mandate under Section 37 is impermissible.
